note: Let k=(a^2+b^2)/(ab+1). Assume a nonsquare k has a positive solution minimizing a+b, with a>=b. If a=b then k<2, hence k=1. Thus a>b. Put c=kb-a. From the equation, a(a-kb)=k-b^2 and ac=b^2-k. If c<=0, then a>=kb. Equality gives k=b^2, contradiction; strict inequality gives a(a-kb)>=a>kb>=k while k-b^2<k, contradiction. Hence c>0. Then ac=b^2-k<b^2 and a>b, so 0<c<b. The quadratic x^2-kbx+b^2-k has roots a,c, hence c^2+b^2=k(bc+1). This produces the smaller positive solution (b,c), contradicting minimality. Proof is self-contained; no predecessor facts needed.
